claim: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (DOA) is a progressive form of blindness caused by degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons.
source: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (DOA) is a progressive form of blindness caused by degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, mainly caused by mutations in the OPA1 mitochondrial dynamin like GTPase (OPA1) gene.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about DOA that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: DOA is mainly caused by mutations in the OPA1 mitochondrial dynamin like GTPase (OPA1) gene.
source: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (DOA) is a progressive form of blindness caused by degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, mainly caused by mutations in the OPA1 mitochondrial dynamin like GTPase (OPA1) gene.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is referenced in the introduction.

claim: OPA1 encodes a dynamin-like GTPase present in the mitochondrial inner membrane.
source: OPA1 encodes a dynamin-like GTPase present in the mitochondrial inner membrane.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about OPA1 protein localization.

claim: DOA plus often results from point mutations in the GTPase domain, which are assumed to have dominant-negative effects.
source: DOA plus often results from point mutations in the GTPase domain, which are assumed to have dominant-negative effects.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about DOA plus mutations.

claim: The presence of mutations in the GTPase domain does not always result in DOA plus.
source: However, the presence of mutations in the GTPase domain does not always result in DOA plus.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of the dOPA1 gene in Drosophila can imitate the pathology of optic nerve degeneration observed in DOA.
source: In this study, we found that loss-of-function mutations of the dOPA1 gene in Drosophila can imitate the pathology of optic nerve degeneration observed in DOA.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human OPA1 (hOPA1) gene expression successfully rescued the degeneration caused by dOPA1 mutations in Drosophila.
source: We successfully rescued this degeneration by expressing the human OPA1 (hOPA1) gene, indicating that hOPA1 is functionally interchangeable with dOPA1 in the fly system.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the rescue experiments.

claim: hOPA1 is functionally interchangeable with dOPA1 in the fly system.
source: We successfully rescued this degeneration by expressing the human OPA1 (hOPA1) gene, indicating that hOPA1 is functionally interchangeable with dOPA1 in the fly system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue experiment results.

claim: Previously identified mutations did not ameliorate the dOPA1 deficiency phenotype.
source: However, mutations previously identified did not ameliorate the dOPA1 deficiency phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the rescue experiments with mutant hOPA1.

claim: DOA plus mutations suppressed the rescue by wild-type hOPA1 when both were expressed in the optic nerve of dOPA1 mutants.
source: By expressing both WT and DOA plus mutant hOPA1 forms in the optic nerve of dOPA1 mutants, we observed that DOA plus mutations suppressed the rescue, facilitating the distinction between loss-of-function and dominant-negative mutations in hOPA1.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from co-expression experiments.

claim: The fly model aids in distinguishing DOA from DOA plus and guides initial hOPA1 mutation treatment strategies.
source: This fly model aids in distinguishing DOA from DOA plus and guides initial hOPA1 mutation treatment strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: DOA has a frequency of 1/12,000 to 1/50,000.
source: Despite being a rare disease with a frequency of 1/12,000 to 1/50,000, DOA is the most commonly diagnosed form of hereditary optic neuropathy.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge about DOA.

claim: DOA is the most commonly diagnosed form of hereditary optic neuropathy.
source: Despite being a rare disease with a frequency of 1/12,000 to 1/50,000, DOA is the most commonly diagnosed form of hereditary optic neuropathy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about DOA.

claim: OPA1 was identified as the causative gene for DOA in 2000.
source: In 2000, OPA1 mitochondrial dynamin like GTPase (OPA1) was identified as the causative gene for DOA (Alexander et al., 2000; Delettre et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: OPA1 is a dynamin-like GTPase located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: OPA1 encodes a dynamin-like GTPase located in the inner mitochondrial membrane (Olichon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: OPA1 has various functions, including mitochondrial fusion, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance, control of cell death, and resistance to reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: It has various functions, including mitochondrial fusion, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance, control of cell death, and resistance to reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Lenaers et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The most common pathogenic mutation in OPA1 is the c.2708–2711 delTTAG deletion.
source: The most common pathogenic mutation in OPA1 is the c.2708–2711 delTTAG deletion (Toomes et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Five pathogenic mutations result in a substantial decrease in OPA1 protein in the fibroblasts from affected patients.
source: Five pathogenic mutations, including the one above, result in a substantial decrease in OPA1 protein in the fibroblasts from affected patients (Zanna et al., 2008), supporting the theory that DOA is caused by haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: DOA is caused by haploinsufficiency.
source: Five pathogenic mutations, including the one above, result in a substantial decrease in OPA1 protein in the fibroblasts from affected patients (Zanna et al., 2008), supporting the theory that DOA is caused by haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is an inference supported by cited research showing decreased protein levels.

claim: Multisystem symptoms have been reported in up to 20% of OPA1 mutation carriers.
source: Optic atrophy is a characteristic feature of OPA1-associated DOA; however, multisystem symptoms have been reported in up to 20% of OPA1 mutation carriers (Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: DOA plus can include sensorineural deafness.
source: DOA plus can include sensorineural deafness (Amati-Bonneau et al., 2008), multiple sclerosis-like illness (Verny et al., 2008; Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2016), parkinsonism and dementia (Carelli et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2017), and cardiomyopathy (Spiegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: DOA plus can include multiple sclerosis-like illness.
source: DOA plus can include sensorineural deafness (Amati-Bonneau et al., 2008), multiple sclerosis-like illness (Verny et al., 2008; Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2016), parkinsonism and dementia (Carelli et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2017), and cardiomyopathy (Spiegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: DOA plus can include parkinsonism and dementia.
source: DOA plus can include sensorineural deafness (Amati-Bonneau et al., 2008), multiple sclerosis-like illness (Verny et al., 2008; Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2016), parkinsonism and dementia (Carelli et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2017), and cardiomyopathy (Spiegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: DOA plus can include cardiomyopathy.
source: DOA plus can include sensorineural deafness (Amati-Bonneau et al., 2008), multiple sclerosis-like illness (Verny et al., 2008; Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2016), parkinsonism and dementia (Carelli et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2017), and cardiomyopathy (Spiegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: The R445H mutation is a well-known mutation associated with DOA plus.
source: The R445H mutation is a well-known mutation associated with DOA plus (Amati-Bonneau et al., 2008; Amati-Bonneau et al., 2003; Shimizu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Missense mutations in the dynamin-featured structure, especially the GTPase domain of OPA1, are more likely to cause severe symptoms compared with loss-of-function mutations such as deletions or splice site mutations.
source: Missense mutations in the dynamin-featured structure, especially the GTPase domain of OPA1, are more likely to cause severe symptoms compared with loss-of-function (LOF) mutations such as deletions or splice site mutations (Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: The severe symptoms from GTPase domain mutations are probably due to the dominant-negative effect on the normal OPA1 allele, since OPA1 functions as a homo-oligomer.
source: This is probably due to the dominant-negative (DN) effect of a DOA plus mutation on the normal OPA1 allele, since OPA1 functions as a homo-oligomer (Frezza et al., 2006; Olichon et al., 2006); in fact, its yeast ortholog, Mgm1, forms oligomers, increasing the GTPase activity (Meglei and McQuibban, 2009; Rujiviphat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations showing OPA1 oligomerization.

claim: The yeast ortholog of OPA1, Mgm1, forms oligomers, increasing the GTPase activity.
source: This is probably due to the dominant-negative (DN) effect of a DOA plus mutation on the normal OPA1 allele, since OPA1 functions as a homo-oligomer (Frezza et al., 2006; Olichon et al., 2006); in fact, its yeast ortholog, Mgm1, forms oligomers, increasing the GTPase activity (Meglei and McQuibban, 2009; Rujiviphat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on yeast Mgm1.

claim: The dynamin-featured structure accounts for 70% of the 233 pathogenic variants of DOA and DOA plus described in the locus-specific database.
source: Particularly, the dynamin-featured structure accounts for 70% of the 233 pathogenic variants of DOA and DOA plus described in the locus-specific database (Ferré et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a database study.

claim: Mutations in the dynamin-featured domains do not determine DOA plus, as it affects only 20% of all OPA1 mutation carriers.
source: However, mutations in these domains do not determine DOA plus, as it affects only 20% of all OPA1 mutation carriers.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations and statistics.

claim: There is currently no effective treatment for DOA or DOA plus.
source: Although currently there is no effective treatment for DOA or DOA plus, distinguishing between them allows earlier planning of interventions such as hearing aids, rather than relying solely on visual aids, necessary only for those with DOA plus.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the current state of treatment.

claim: Distinguishing between DOA and DOA plus allows earlier planning of interventions such as hearing aids.
source: Although currently there is no effective treatment for DOA or DOA plus, distinguishing between them allows earlier planning of interventions such as hearing aids, rather than relying solely on visual aids, necessary only for those with DOA plus.
evidence: This is an inference about the clinical utility of distinguishing between the two conditions.

claim: Precedents exist in simpler systems such as yeast and human fibroblasts for differentiating between LOF and DN effects.
source: In the quest to differentiate between LOF and DN effects within the context of genetic mutations, precedents exist in simpler systems such as yeast and human fibroblasts. These models have provided valuable insights into the conserved functions of OPA1 across species, as evidenced by studies in yeast models (Del Dotto et al., 2017) and fibroblasts derived from patients harboring OPA1 mutations (Kane et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research in yeast and fibroblasts.

claim: The ability to distinguish between LOF and DN effects in an in vivo model organism, particularly at the structural level of retinal axon degeneration, has remained elusive.
source: However, the ability to distinguish between LOF and DN effects in an in vivo model organism, particularly at the structural level of retinal axon degeneration, has remained elusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of prior models discussed in the manuscript.

claim: DOA models have been reported in vertebrates such as mice and zebrafish, simple organisms such as nematodes and fruit flies, and in vitro yeast and cultured cell models.
source: As OPA1 is conserved in various species, DOA models have been reported in vertebrates such as mice and zebrafish, simple organisms such as nematodes and fruit flies, and in vitro yeast and cultured cell models (Del Dotto and Carelli, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In mouse models, focal RGC axons decrease in number with mitochondrial abnormalities at the electron microscope level, but the phenotype appears slowly.
source: In mouse models, focal RGC axons decrease in number with mitochondrial abnormalities at the electron microscope level, but the phenotype appears slowly, not allowing for analysis in a short time frame (Alavi et al., 2007; Davies et al., 2007; Nguyen et al., 2011; Sarzi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mouse model studies.

claim: Zebrafish models have displayed developmental delays in eyes and heads, short length, and body axis abnormalities.
source: Zebrafish models have displayed developmental delays in eyes and heads, short length, and body axis abnormalities (Eijkenboom et al., 2019; Rahn et al., 2013) but have not been used to investigate optic nerve degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior zebrafish studies.

claim: Zebrafish models have not been used to investigate optic nerve degeneration.
source: Zebrafish models have displayed developmental delays in eyes and heads, short length, and body axis abnormalities (Eijkenboom et al., 2019; Rahn et al., 2013) but have not been used to investigate optic nerve degeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, most studies focused on muscle cells using mutants of eat-3, an OPA1 homolog.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, most studies focused on muscle cells using mutants of eat-3, an OPA1 homolog (Kanazawa et al., 2008; Rolland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior C. elegans studies.

claim: The mitochondria in the posterior lateral microtubule neurons of C. elegans did not show any difference in size from its wild-type counterparts.
source: However, the mitochondria in the posterior lateral microtubule neurons did not show any difference in size from its wild-type (WT) counterparts (Byrne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LOF of eat-3 may have a limited impact on phenotypic outcomes in the nervous system of C. elegans.
source: Thus, LOF of eat-3 may have a limited impact on phenotypic outcomes in the nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited observation of no mitochondrial size difference.

claim: A DOA model in which hOpa1K301A is expressed in GABAergic motor neurons of C. elegans showed a decreased number of mitochondria in those cells.
source: Nevertheless, a DOA model in which hOPA1K301A is expressed in GABAergic motor neurons showed a decreased number of mitochondria in those cells (Zaninello et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The dOPA1 somatic clone in the Drosophila eye exhibited a rough-eye phenotype, eye structural abnormalities, and increased MitoSOX fluorescence.
source: In a fly model, the dOPA1 somatic clone in the eye exhibited a rough-eye phenotype, eye structural abnormalities, and increased MitoSOX fluorescence, which was partially rescued by vitamin E or SOD1 expression (Yarosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior Drosophila research.

claim: The rough-eye phenotype and increased MitoSOX fluorescence in dOPA1 somatic clones was partially rescued by vitamin E or SOD1 expression.
source: In a fly model, the dOPA1 somatic clone in the eye exhibited a rough-eye phenotype, eye structural abnormalities, and increased MitoSOX fluorescence, which was partially rescued by vitamin E or SOD1 expression (Yarosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Heterozygous dOPA1 mutants showed shortened lifespan, elevated ROS levels, and irregular muscle tissue mitochondrial structures.
source: Heterozygous dOPA1 mutants showed shortened lifespan, elevated ROS levels, and irregular muscle tissue mitochondrial structures (Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The electroretinogram pattern in heterozygous dOPA1 mutants showed age-dependent decreases in the on-transient response, heart rate, negative geotaxis response, and increased heart arrhythmia due to heat shock stress.
source: Moreover, the electroretinogram pattern showed age-dependent decreases in the on-transient response, heart rate, negative geotaxis response, and increased heart arrhythmia due to heat shock stress (Shahrestani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Except for mice, the evidence of optic nerve axonal abnormalities is limited in model organisms such as zebrafish, worms, and flies.
source: However, except for mice, the evidence of optic nerve axonal abnormalities is limited in model organisms such as zebrafish, worms, and flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of prior literature.

claim: The structure of the Drosophila visual system is similar to that of mammals.
source: The structure of the Drosophila visual system is similar to that of mammals (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010), with conserved mechanisms of synaptogenesis and neural circuit formation (Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Drosophila has conserved mechanisms of synaptogenesis and neural circuit formation with mammals.
source: The structure of the Drosophila visual system is similar to that of mammals (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010), with conserved mechanisms of synaptogenesis and neural circuit formation (Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Drosophila photoreceptors type R7/8 extend their retinal axons from the retina directly into the brain, forming synapses in the second optic ganglion medulla via the chiasma.
source: Drosophila photoreceptors type R7/8 extend their retinal axons from the retina directly into the brain, forming synapses in the second optic ganglion medulla via the chiasma (Figure 1A), having potential application as a model for mammalian photoreceptors and RGCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila visual system anatomy, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Drosophila photoreceptors have potential application as a model for mammalian photoreceptors and RGCs.
source: Drosophila photoreceptors type R7/8 extend their retinal axons from the retina directly into the brain, forming synapses in the second optic ganglion medulla via the chiasma (Figure 1A), having potential application as a model for mammalian photoreceptors and RGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarities discussed.

claim: The retinal axons of Drosophila are defined as analogous to the human optic nerve in this study.
source: In this study, we defined the retinal axons of Drosophila as analogous to the human optic nerve.
evidence: This is an explicit methodological definition made by the authors.

claim: dOPA1 colocalizes with mitochondria in retinal axons.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that the HA signals colocalized with mCherry-mito in the axon terminals of photoreceptor cells (Figure 1B). This indicated that dOPA1 colocalizes with mitochondria in retinal axons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using confocal microscopy.

claim: The intensity of the mitochondrial signal was significantly reduced in the retinal axons of dOPA1 RNAi flies.
source: The intensity of the mitochondrial signal was significantly reduced in the retinal axons of these flies (Figure 1C and D; quantification in Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C, D, and E.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial transport was previously reported in the LOF of marf (MFN 1/2 homolog), which is necessary for the fusion of the outer membrane of mitochondria.
source: Previously, impaired mitochondrial transport was reported in the LOF of marf (MFN 1/2 homolog), which is necessary for the fusion of the outer membrane of mitochondria (Sandoval et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Both dOPA1 knockdown and control flies showed mitochondrial signals in the axon terminals at 24 hr after puparium formation.
source: Both dOPA1 knockdown and control flies showed mitochondrial signals in the axon terminals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No mitochondrial signals were observed in the axon terminals of flies with a knockdown of milton.
source: However, no mitochondrial signals were observed in the axon terminals of flies with a knockdown of milton, which is thought to act as an adaptor between kinesin to mitochondria, promoting anterograde transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Milton is thought to act as an adaptor between kinesin to mitochondria, promoting anterograde transport.
source: However, no mitochondrial signals were observed in the axon terminals of flies with a knockdown of milton, which is thought to act as an adaptor between kinesin to mitochondria, promoting anterograde transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about milton function.

claim: Trafficking defects are not the main cause of the mitochondrial mislocalization observed in the retinal axons of the dOPA1 knockdown.
source: These findings suggest that trafficking defects are not the main cause of the mitochondrial mislocalization observed in the retinal axons of the dOPA1 knockdown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with milton knockdown results.

claim: The dOPA1 knockdown led to a significant decrease in mitochondrial size in R1–6 axons.
source: The dOPA1 knockdown led to a significant decrease in mitochondrial size in R1–6 axons (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: There was significant heterogeneity in healthy mitochondria, ranging from dense matrix (Class A) to swollen mitochondria with a hypodense matrix (Class B).
source: In addition, there was significant heterogeneity in healthy mitochondria, ranging from dense matrix (Class A) to swollen mitochondria with a hypodense matrix (Class B) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Knocking down dOpa1 in R1–6 axon terminals resulted in severely abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure (22.8%).
source: Knocking down dOpa1 in R1–6 axon terminals resulted in severely abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure (22.8%; Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: dOPA1 is involved in maintaining proper mitochondrial morphology by promoting mitochondrial fusion in retinal axons.
source: These results suggest that dOPA1 is involved in maintaining proper mitochondrial morphology by promoting mitochondrial fusion in retinal axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mitochondrial fragmentation observed in dOPA1 knockdown.

claim: ROS levels were significantly elevated in dOPA1 knockdown retinal axons compared to control.
source: The results showed significantly elevated ROS levels in dOPA1 knockdown retinal axons compared to control (Figure 2A and B; quantification in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MitoSOX shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: An increase in mitophagy activity has been reported in mouse RGCs and nematode ADOA models.
source: Given that an increase in mitophagy activity has been reported in mouse RGCs and nematode ADOA models (Zaninello et al., 2022; Zaninello et al., 2020), the mitoQC marker, an established indicator of mitophagy activity, was expressed in the photoreceptors of Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Post dOPA1 knockdown, there was a significant elevation in mCherry-positive and GFP-negative puncta signals at 1 week, demonstrating an activation of mitophagy.
source: Post dOPA1 knockdown, we observed a significant elevation in mCherry-positive and GFP-negative puncta signals at 1 week, demonstrating an activation of mitophagy as a consequence of dOPA1 knockdown (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using the mitoQC reporter shown in Figures 2D-H.

claim: The dOPA1 knockdown caused axonal degeneration 1 day after eclosion, further decreasing 1 week later.
source: Our results showed that the dOPA1 knockdown caused axonal degeneration 1 day after eclosion, further decreasing 1 week later (Figure 3B–E, quantification in Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MeDUsA quantification shown in Figures 3B-F.

claim: Similar results were obtained with an independent alternative RNAi line for dOPA1.
source: We obtained similar results with an independent alternative RNAi line (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dOPA1 knockdown caused a significant decrease in the number of rhabdomeres per ommatidium in 1-week-old adults.
source: The dOPA1 knockdown caused a significant decrease in the number of rhabdomeres per ommatidium in 1-week-old adults (Figure 3G–J, quantification in Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy shown in Figures 3G-K.

claim: Although the retinal axons had already decreased on the day of eclosion, the ommatidia remained intact.
source: Interestingly, although the retinal axons had already decreased on the day of eclosion, the ommatidia remained intact (Figure 3F and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and K.

claim: The ommatidia in R7 remained intact after 1 week in dOPA1 knockdown flies.
source: Note that the ommatidia in R7 remained intact after 1 week (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The dOPA1 knockdown causes degeneration in both axonal terminals and cell bodies, with the neuronal degeneration starting from the axons and continuing in the cell bodies.
source: Our results indicate that the dOPA1 knockdown causes degeneration in both axonal terminals and cell bodies, with the neuronal degeneration starting from the axons and continuing in the cell bodies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal pattern of degeneration observed in the data.

claim: The compound eyes of homozygous mutations of dOPA1 displayed a glossy eye phenotype.
source: A previous report indicated that the compound eyes of homozygous mutations of dOPA1 displayed a glossy eye phenotype (Yarosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Upon knocking down dOPA1 using the GMR-Gal4 driver, a glossy eye-like rough-eye phenotype was observed in the compound eyes.
source: Upon knocking down dOPA1 using the GMR-Gal4 driver, we also observed a glossy eye-like rough-eye phenotype in the compound eyes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significantly lower number of dOPA1 mutant retinal axons than in controls was found 1 day after eclosion.
source: Using MeDUsA, we found a significantly lower number of dOPA1 mutant retinal axons than in controls 1 day after eclosion (Figure 4A and B, quantification in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutant clone analysis shown in Figures 4A, B, and D.

claim: dOPA1 expression partially rescued the axonal degeneration in dOPA1 eye clone flies at 1 day after eclosion.
source: To determine if dOPA1 is responsible for axon neurodegeneration, we quantify the number of the axons in the dOPA1 eye clone fly with the expression of dOPA1 at 1 day after eclosion and found that dOPA1 expression partially rescued the axonal degeneration (Figure 4C, quantification in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: dOPA1 is necessary for maintaining the number of retinal axons in the Drosophila visual system.
source: Our results indicate that dOPA1 is necessary for maintaining the number of retinal axons in the Drosophila visual system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant and rescue experiment results.

claim: The neurodegeneration observed in the LOF of dOPA1 is due to the progressive loss of retinal axons, as well as the mammal optic nerve.
source: In conclusion, the neurodegeneration observed in the LOF of dOPA1 is due to the progressive loss of retinal axons, as well as the mammal optic nerve.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the Drosophila model to mammalian optic nerve degeneration.

claim: Observations in dOPA1 LOF flies confirmed mitochondrial fragmentation, increased ROS levels, and degeneration of retinal axons, as reported in mammals.
source: Our observations in dOPA1 LOF flies confirmed mitochondrial fragmentation, increased ROS levels, and degeneration of retinal axons, as reported in mammals.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings compared to mammalian studies.

claim: The function of OPA1 may be conserved across Drosophila and humans.
source: These data indicated that the function of OPA1 may be conserved across Drosophila and humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of phenotypes between flies and mammals.

claim: hOPA1 expression in the retinal axons of the dOPA1 mutant partially rescued the number of axons.
source: Using this UAS-hOPA1, we performed rescue experiments. hOPA1 expression in the retinal axons of the dOPA1 mutant, which generated somatic cell clones, partially rescued the number of axons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: hOPA1 and dOPA1 are interchangeable.
source: These results suggest that hOPA1 and dOPA1 are interchangeable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment results.

claim: The expression of hOPA1 mutations 2708-2711del, I382M, D438V, and R445H in retinal axons failed to rescue the dOPA1 deficiency to the same extent as the WT hOPA1.
source: The expression of these mutations in retinal axons failed to rescue the dOPA1 deficiency to the same extent as the WT hOPA1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Unlike the D438V and R445H mutations, the 2708-2711del and I382M mutations could be weakly rescued.
source: Importantly, unlike the D438V and R445H mutations, the 2708-2711del and I382M mutations could be weakly rescued.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing rescue efficiencies.

claim: The 2708-2711del and I382M mutations result in LOF, but may retain some residual activity.
source: This suggests that these mutations result in LOF, but may retain some residual activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial rescue observed.

claim: The findings are in line with the observed severity of the associated diseases, DOA and DOA plus.
source: These findings are also in line with the observed severity of the associated diseases, DOA and DOA plus.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental results to clinical observations.

claim: WT hOPA1 effectively mitigated the ROS phenotype, whereas the 2708-2711del, D438V, and R445H mutants did not.
source: Similar to its effect on axonal degeneration, WT hOPA1 effectively mitigated the phenotype, whereas the 2708-2711del, D438V, and R445H mutants did not (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The I382M variant also reduced ROS levels comparably to the WT.
source: Importantly, the I382M variant also reduced ROS levels comparably to the WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on ROS measurements.

claim: Both axonal degeneration and the increase in ROS caused by dOPA1 downregulation can be effectively counteracted by hOPA1.
source: These findings demonstrate that both axonal degeneration and the increase in ROS caused by dOPA1 downregulation can be effectively counteracted by hOPA1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment results.

claim: I382M retains partial functionality and acts as a relatively weak hypomorph in this experimental setup.
source: Although I382M retains partial functionality, it acts as a relatively weak hypomorph in this experimental setup.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial rescue observed with I382M.

claim: The expression of the WT, 2708del, and I382M did not result in any changes when rescued by hOPA1 substitution in the co-expression experiment.
source: As a result, the expression of the WT, 2708del, and I382M did not result in any changes when rescued by hOPA1 substitution (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.
